claim: AWS WAF can protect web sites that are not hosted in AWS, because it is integrated with Amazon CloudFront, which supports custom origins outside of AWS.
question: Can AWS WAF protect a web site that is not hosted in AWS?

values.display: supports custom origins outside of AWS

evidence.quote: Yes, AWS WAF is integrated with Amazon CloudFront, which supports custom origins outside of AWS.

claim: A rate-based rule is like a regular AWS WAF rule, with one addition: the ability to configure a rate-based threshold.
question: How does an AWS WAF rate-based rule differ from a regular rule?

values.display: the ability to configure a rate-based threshold

evidence.quote: Rate-based Rules are similar to regular Rules, with one addition: the ability to configure a rate-based threshold.

claim: A rate-based rule can also contain any other AWS WAF condition that is available for a regular rule.
question: Can a rate-based rule also hold other match conditions, such as a URI match?

evidence.quote: A Rate-based Rule can also contain any other AWS WAF Condition that is available for a regular rule.

note: d116; waf#17; see also waf#20 and waf#23 (limit a login page)

claim: The AWS WAF FAQ describes a rate-based rule as setting the number of web requests allowed by a client IP in a trailing, continuously updated, 5 minute period.
question: Over what time period does the AWS WAF FAQ say a rate-based rule counts requests?

evidence.quote: Rate-based Rules are type of Rule that can be configured in AWS WAF, allowing you to specify the number of web requests that are allowed by a client IP in a trailing, continuously updated, 5 minute period.

note: waf#16; FAQ wording. The Developer Guide rate-based pages describe other evaluation windows and aggregation keys besides client IP: the numbers lens facts are the current truth; let the conflict queue compare.

claim: If an IP address breaches the configured limit of a rate-based rule, new requests are blocked until the request rate falls below the configured threshold.
question: Does a rate-based rule keep blocking an IP address after its request rate drops?

values.display: until the request rate falls below the configured threshold

evidence.quote: If an IP address breaches the configured limit, new requests will be blocked until the request rate falls below the configured threshold.

claim: AWS WAF rate-based rules are designed to protect against use cases such as web-layer DDoS attacks, brute force login attempts and bad bots.
question: Can an AWS WAF rate-based rule help mitigate web-layer DDoS attacks?

evidence.quote: This new rules type is designed to protect you from use cases such web-layer DDoS attacks, brute force login attempts and bad bots.

claim: You can exempt high-traffic source IP ranges from being blocked by a rate-based rule by having a separate IP match condition that allows the request within the rate-based rule.
question: Can certain high-traffic source IP ranges be exempted from a rate-based rule?

evidence.quote: You can do this by having a separate IP match condition that allows the request within the Rate-base Rule.

note: d118; waf#24 (the quote answers the question "Can I exempt certain high-traffic source IP ranges from being blocked by my Rate-based Rule(s)?")

claim: After an initial setup, adding or changing AWS WAF rules typically takes around a minute to propagate worldwide.
question: How long does a change to AWS WAF rules take to propagate?

values.display: typically takes around a minute to propagate worldwide

evidence.quote: After an initial setup, adding or changing to rules typically takes around a minute to propagate worldwide.

claim: AWS WAF can inspect web requests transmitted over HTTP or HTTPS.
question: Can AWS WAF inspect HTTPS traffic?

evidence.quote: AWS WAF helps protect applications and can inspect web requests transmitted over HTTP or HTTPS.

claim: AWS WAF application layer (L7) DDoS protection can be purchased standalone and does not require an AWS Shield Advanced subscription.
question: Do you need AWS Shield Advanced to use the AWS WAF application layer DDoS protection rule group?

values.display: does not require an AWS Shield Advanced subscription

evidence.quote: AWS WAF application layer (L7) DDoS protection can be purchased standalone and does not require an AWS Shield Advanced subscription.

note: d121; waf#69; feature added after mid-2022 (date not stated on the FAQ; the numbers+changes lens records the date)

claim: AWS WAF application layer (L7) DDoS protection is an AWS Managed Rule group designed to automatically defend applications against DDoS events within seconds.
question: What is AWS WAF application layer DDoS protection?

evidence.quote: AWS WAF application layer (L7) DDoS protection is an AWS Managed Rule group that is designed to automatically defend applications against distributed denial of service (DDoS) events within seconds.

claim: Resources on Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer and API Gateway are currently protected by AWS WAF application layer DDoS protection.
question: Which resources can use the AWS WAF application layer DDoS protection rule group?

values.display: Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer (ALB) and API Gateway

evidence.quote: Currently, resources on Amazon CloudFront, Application Load Balancer (ALB) and API Gateway are protected by this feature.

note: waf#57; the display is a resource list copied from the quote

claim: The application layer DDoS protection AWS Managed Rule group adds 50 WCUs to the WCU count in AWS WAF.
question: How many WCUs does the application layer DDoS protection rule group add to a web ACL?

qualifiers.scope: per web ACL that uses the rule group

evidence.quote: Yes, by 50 WCUs.

note: waf#65 (question: "Will this AWS Managed Rule group add to the WCU count in AWS WAF? If so, by how much?")

claim: AWS WAF can inspect HTTP/S requests coming from both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.
question: Does AWS WAF support IPv6?

evidence.quote: Yes, support for IPv6 allows the AWS WAF to inspect HTTP/S requests coming from both IPv6 and IPv4 addresses.

claim: The AWS WAF FAQ lists Amazon CloudFront, the Application Load Balancer (ALB), Amazon API Gateway and AWS AppSync as the services AWS WAF can be deployed on.
question: Which AWS services does the AWS WAF FAQ say AWS WAF can be deployed on?

values.display: Amazon API Gateway, and AWS AppSync

evidence.quote: AWS WAF can be deployed on Amazon CloudFront, the Application Load Balancer (ALB), Amazon API Gateway, and AWS AppSync.

note: d122; waf#12. The Developer Guide list of protected resource types is longer (for example Amazon Cognito user pools, AWS App Runner, AWS Verified Access, AWS Amplify): the guide is current truth.

claim: As part of Amazon API Gateway, AWS WAF can help secure and protect REST APIs.
question: Which kind of Amazon API Gateway API does AWS WAF protect?

evidence.quote: As part of Amazon API Gateway, it can help secure and protect your REST APIs.

claim: As part of AWS AppSync, AWS WAF can help secure and protect GraphQL APIs.
question: Can AWS WAF protect GraphQL APIs?

evidence.quote: As part of AWS AppSync, it can help secure and protect your GraphQL APIs.

claim: When you use AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront, your rules run in all AWS edge locations, close to your end users.
question: Where do AWS WAF rules run when the web ACL is on a CloudFront distribution?

values.display: your rules run in all AWS Edge Locations

evidence.quote: When you use AWS WAF on Amazon CloudFront, your rules run in all AWS Edge Locations, located around the world close to your end users.

claim: When you use AWS WAF on regional services such as Application Load Balancer, Amazon API Gateway and AWS AppSync, your rules run in the Region and can protect internet-facing resources as well as internal resources.
question: Can AWS WAF on a regional resource such as an ALB protect internal (not internet-facing) resources?

values.display: internet-facing resources as well as internal resources

evidence.quote: When you use AWS WAF on regional services, such as Application Load Balancer, Amazon API Gateway, and AWS AppSync, your rules run in region and can be used to protect internet-facing resources as well as internal resources.

claim: Requests that AWS WAF blocks are stopped before they reach your web servers.
question: Do requests that AWS WAF blocks reach the origin web servers?

values.display: stopped before they reach your web servers

evidence.quote: Blocked requests are stopped before they reach your web servers.

claim: AWS WAF Sampled Web Requests are stored for up to 3 hours.
question: How long does AWS WAF keep sampled web requests?

evidence.quote: Sampled Web Requests are stored for up to 3 hours.

claim: AWS WAF offers two ways to see how a website is being protected: one-minute metrics in CloudWatch and Sampled Web Requests in the AWS WAF API or management console.
question: How can you see whether AWS WAF rules are working?

values.display: one-minute metrics are available in CloudWatch

evidence.quote: AWS WAF includes two different ways to see how your website is being protected: one-minute metrics are available in CloudWatch and Sampled Web Requests are available in the AWS WAF API or management console.
